analysis.one_liner: Halts new mountaintop removal coal mining permits until federal health studies are done.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in three House committees without a single vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required federal health agencies to run comprehensive studies on whether mountaintop removal coal mining in Kentucky, Tennessee, West Virginia, and Virginia is harming nearby residents' health. Until the Health and Human Services Secretary published a finding that the mining poses no health risk, no federal or state agency could issue a new permit or permit expansion for such mining. Existing projects would have to monitor air, water, noise, and soil pollution continuously, with results posted publicly, and a one-time fee on mining companies would cover the cost of the studies.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities surrounding mountaintop removal sites in Appalachia, who would get federally funded health studies, a public database of pollution monitoring, and a pause on new mining permits until health risks were assessed.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences to conduct comprehensive studies of the health impacts of mountaintop removal mining on surrounding communities, with results made public.

Blocks issuance of any new permit or permit expansion for mountaintop removal under the Clean Water Act or the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act until HHS publishes a determination that the mining poses no health risk.

Requires companies running existing mountaintop removal projects to continuously monitor air, water, noise, and soil pollution and submit results monthly, which HHS must post in a searchable public database within seven days.

Cites peer-reviewed research finding elevated rates of birth defects, hospitalizations for chronic pulmonary disorders and hypertension, lung cancer, and mortality in mining counties that persist after controlling for other variables.

analysis.who_pays: Coal companies conducting mountaintop removal mining, which would pay a one-time fee covering the studies and monitoring, and would be unable to get new or expanded permits until the health determination is issued. Coal-dependent counties could also lose the jobs and tax base that new mining projects would have brought during the study period.

drawbacks.text: The permit moratorium takes effect immediately and lasts indefinitely, since it ends only after studies are completed and HHS publishes a determination, which could take years and cost jobs in counties where mining is a main employer.

It pauses new permits before the science is settled: the bill's own findings call the evidence 'initial' and justify the moratorium on the basis of concern, so a fair-minded critic could argue regulators should wait for proof before shutting down an industry.
Mining operators must fund continuous air, water, noise, and soil monitoring and a one-time federal fee, compliance costs that would likely be passed through to coal buyers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people living beside mountaintop removal sites, the bill offered something they currently lack: an independent federal answer on whether the mining is making them sick, plus a pause on new permits in the meantime. The cost is real but bounded: existing mines could keep operating, only new and expanded permits were frozen, and the industry itself would fund the studies. The heaviest cost falls on coal-dependent communities that would forgo new mining jobs during the study period, and the indefinite, proof-not-required-until-clean structure was the bill's most contestable design choice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then three subcommittees, none of which ever took it up, so it never reached the House floor for a vote and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Yarmuth introduced the ACHE Act on February 6, 2013, with 23 original cosponsors.
The Speaker referred the bill to three committees — Natural Resources, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Energy and Commerce — meaning it needed action from multiple committees to advance.
Within ten days it was sent to three subcommittees: Water Resources and Environment, Environment and the Economy, and Energy and Mineral Resources.

No committee or subcommittee ever held a markup, reported the bill, or brought it to the floor; the complete action history ends with the February 2013 subcommittee referrals, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
The bill gathered 46 cosponsors, all Democrats, and had no Republican support and no Senate companion action in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mountaintop removal operators were better off: no new health studies were mandated, no monitoring requirements or fees were imposed, and new and expanded mining permits continued to be issued without any health-risk determination. Residents near mining sites gained nothing and kept waiting for the federal health assessment the bill would have produced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal operators and permitting status quo

sides.party_line_note: All 46 cosponsors were Democrats and there were no Republican cosponsors; the bill never reached a roll call, so no votes were recorded.

industries.note: The bill would freeze new and expanded permits for their operations until a federal health determination, and charge them a fee for the studies and continuous pollution monitoring. The industry's interest in continuing to permit without a health assessment runs directly against residents' interest in knowing whether the mining is making them sick.

A pause on new mining permits would delay jobs and tax revenue in counties where mining is a main employer. Many of those same counties are where residents would benefit most from the health studies, so the burden and the benefit land on the same communities.
